introduction: This guide is about why the Bahá’í writings contain laws and how a believer is meant to stand toward them. The readings call the laws lamps of loving providence and a fortress, say they are to be kept for love and not from fear, compare them to a physician’s remedy fitted to its time, record how the Most Holy Book was revealed and how earlier ordinances were kept or set aside, and ask again and again that people act on what they have been given. The quotations beside them come from traditions that love law, among them Deuteronomy, the Psalms, the Qur’an and the rabbis, and from thinkers who tied law to freedom, such as Aristotle, Locke and Rousseau. Others speak for the misgivings: Paul on the letter that kills, Augustine’s “love, and do what you will”, Confucius on the limits of rule by statute, and Emerson, who would own no law but his own nature.
questions: The readings describe the laws as lamps of loving providence and as a fortress. Which of the laws you know have you experienced as protection, and which have you had to learn to see that way?
Locke and the Psalmist both tie law to liberty. What kind of freedom do the readings promise, and how does it differ from doing as one pleases?
Paul warns that the letter kills, and Jesus that small rules can crowd out judgment, mercy and faith. How do the readings guard against that danger?
Several readings explain that laws are revealed gradually and applied with wisdom. What does that suggest about how to speak of law with someone new to it?
Confucius thought that people led by statutes merely avoid punishment. What, in these readings, makes obedience an act of love and not of fear?
The last readings join obedience with submission and with reason. Where does your own judgment come in when you follow a law you do not yet understand?

outside.why: Moses sums up what God requires and adds the reason: these commandments are given for thy good.
Jesus joins love and law in seven words: if ye love me, keep my commandments.
Proverbs already calls the commandment a lamp and the law a light, as this reading calls the laws lamps of loving providence.
James speaks of a perfect law of liberty, in which the one who continues is blessed in what he does.
The psalmist finds that keeping the precepts is what lets him walk at liberty.
John Locke argued that the end of law is to preserve and enlarge freedom: where there is no law there is no freedom.
Jesus also holds recognition and practice together: not everyone who says Lord, Lord, but the one who does the will.
Emerson declared that no law could be sacred to him but that of his own nature. What does this reading say to a person who trusts only the law within?
Rousseau held that appetite is slavery, and that liberty is obedience to a law we prescribe to ourselves. Can a law given by another become one's own, and how?
James makes the same demand of his readers: be doers of the word, and not hearers only.
Jesus asks that a person's good works be the light others see.
The Qur’an asks for a community that invites to goodness, enjoins right conduct and forbids indecency.
Milton, arguing against the suppression of books, wrote that whoever destroys a good book kills reason itself.
Paul says that the commandments are summed up in loving one's neighbour: love is the fulfilling of the law.
Jesus gives one rule as the whole of the law and the prophets: do to others as you would have them do to you.
The psalm praises the law as perfect, converting the soul, rejoicing the heart, enlightening the eyes.
Joshua is told that the book of the law should not depart from his mouth, and that he should meditate on it day and night.
Paul wrote that the letter kills, but the spirit gives life. How does a person keep the utmost regard for ordinances without making the letter everything?
Jesus likens the one who hears and does his sayings to a house built on rock, which the floods could not move.
The psalmist speaks of the law as of something loved: it is his meditation all the day.
The psalmist asks for his eyes to be opened so that he may see wondrous things in the law.
The first letter of John says that this is the love of God, that we keep His commandments, and they are not grievous.
Deuteronomy asks that the words be in the heart and spoken of at home and on the road, at lying down and at rising.
Jesus says that whoever breaks the least of the commandments, and teaches others to, shall be called least.
Augustine gave a daring short rule: love, and do what you will. Does the mystic who has reached love still need the law, as this reading insists?
Paul describes the struggle exactly: he delights in the law of God inwardly, and finds another law at war in his members.
Aristotle held that to let law rule is to let God and reason rule, for the law is reason unaffected by desire.
The Qur’an says that for each community God appointed a law and a way, and tells them to vie in good works.
These are the commandments of Sinai, which the reading says every Manifestation renews.
Paul observes that people who never received the law do by nature what it contains, showing it written in their hearts.
Antigone appeals to unwritten and unfailing statutes that are not of today or yesterday, and no one knows when they were first put forth.
The Qur’an says that both the creation and the commandment belong to God.
The Tao Te Ching speaks of a Way that all things depend on, not one refusing obedience to it.
The Qur’an tells believers to obey God and the Messenger, and to refer to them whatever they dispute about.
Moses says that the commandment is not hidden or far off, but very near, in the mouth and in the heart.
Jesus said that the sabbath was made for man and not man for the sabbath. How should that saying guide someone unsure how a particular law applies?
Jesus rebuked those who tithed herbs and neglected judgment, mercy and faith. How do detailed ordinances keep their place beside the weightier matters?
Paul tells the Colossians not to let anyone judge them in food, drink or holy days, which are a shadow of things to come.
Isaiah gives his hearers a test for every teaching: to the law and to the testimony.
Paul ends his argument in wonder at a wisdom whose judgments are unsearchable.
Moses was forty days and nights on the mountain, without bread or water, writing the words of the covenant.
Jesus says the same of his own words: I have not spoken of myself; the Father gave me a commandment what I should say.
Moses tells Israel that other nations, hearing these statutes, will call them a wise and understanding people.
Jesus held some things back from his disciples because they could not bear them yet.
Isaiah foresees many peoples going up to learn, for out of Zion shall go forth the law.
The first psalm calls that person blessed whose delight is in the law and who meditates in it day and night.
The psalmist says the statutes have been his songs in the house of his pilgrimage.
Deuteronomy distinguishes what is secret from what is revealed, and says the revealed things are ours so that we may do them.
The Letter to the Hebrews argues that by speaking of a new covenant God made the first one old.
Jesus said he had not come to destroy the law but to fulfil it, yet much was changed. Is a book that abrogates earlier ones an ending or a fulfilment?
In Deuteronomy even the king must write out a copy of the law and read it all his days.
Burke observed that a state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation. How do an unchangeable foundation and a body able to legislate serve each other?
Isaiah describes teaching that comes precept upon precept, line upon line, here a little and there a little.
Paul thinks of law as given at its proper time, like a schoolmaster for a stage of growth.
Paul fed the Corinthians with milk and not meat, because they were not yet able to bear it.
The Qur’an, in laying down the fast, excuses the sick and the traveller and says that God desires ease and not hardship.
Micah's answer joins practice and character: do justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with thy God.
The Qur’an says that no verse is abrogated or caused to be forgotten without something better or like it being brought.
Samuel tells a king who had kept back spoil for offerings that to obey is better than sacrifice.
The Preacher's conclusion is brief: fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.
Ezekiel says that when the wicked turn from their wickedness and do what is lawful and right, they shall live.
The Letter to the Hebrews calls the earlier law a shadow of good things to come.
Isaiah's fast is to loose the bands of wickedness and let the oppressed go free. What does an outward fast need, to be the fast he describes?
The Qur’an says that God effaces what He will and confirms what He will, and with Him is the source of ordinance.
The Qur’an lists giving wealth to kin, orphans and the needy, and paying the poor-due, among the marks of righteousness.
Jesus likens a well-taught scribe to a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old.
Malachi tells the people to bring their tithes into the storehouse and see whether heaven does not open its windows.
The Qur’an says that God tasks no soul beyond its scope, a principle that shapes how its particular rulings are framed.
Moses forbids adding to the word that is commanded or taking from it.
A saying of Muhammad encourages treatment: God created no disease without creating its remedy.
James says that mercy rejoices against judgment. Why would one who longs to forgive still hold himself bound by the law?
Leviticus says of the statutes that a person who does them shall live in them.
Proverbs says that where there is no vision the people perish, but that the one who keeps the law is happy.
Jeremiah foresees a law put in the inward parts and written on the heart.
Kant named two things that fill the mind with awe: the starry heavens above and the moral law within.
Confucius thought that people led by laws and punishments avoid penalty and have no shame, while those led by virtue become good. What makes observing a law more than avoiding its penalty?
Jesus asks the question plainly: why call me Lord, Lord, and do not the things I say?
Proverbs praises a woman clothed with strength and honour, in whose tongue is the law of kindness.
Proverbs promises the child who keeps the commandments length of days, long life and peace.
The psalmist has hidden the word in his heart so that he might not sin.
Paul says it is not the hearers of the law who are just before God, but the doers.
Jesus charges the teachers of his day with laying aside the commandment of God to keep their own tradition.
Aristotle thought that a human being is the best of animals when perfected, and the worst when separated from law and justice.
The first letter to Timothy names the purpose of the commandment: charity out of a pure heart and a good conscience.
Paul concluded that a person is justified by faith without the deeds of the law. In what sense can commandments be the cause of salvation?
Paul asks those who are spiritual to restore the one who has fallen, gently, and so to fulfil the law of Christ.
Rabbi Tarfon used to say that the day is short and the work is plentiful, and the master of the house is pressing.
The Dhammapada compares one who recites much of the law and does not practise it to a cowherd counting another's cattle.
George Herbert thought that sweeping a room as for God's laws makes the room and the action fine.
The voice from the whirlwind asks Job whether he knows the ordinances of heaven.
The Qur’an tells the believers to hold fast, all together, to the cable of God and not to separate.
The Qur’an also speaks of a covenant that God made with the prophets.
Ezekiel hears the promise of a new heart and a new spirit, so that the people will walk in the statutes.
Jesus says that if parents know how to give good gifts, how much more will the Father give to those who ask.
Wordsworth, praising the sonnet's narrow room, says that the prison to which we doom ourselves is no prison.
The prayer Jesus taught includes the same surrender: Thy will be done.
Ignatius of Loyola prayed: take, Lord, and receive all my liberty, my memory, my understanding and my whole will.
Paul tells the Philippians to work out their own salvation with fear and trembling, since it is God who works in them.
Socrates told the court that he honoured and loved them, but would obey God rather than them.
Locke held that reason must be our last judge and guide in everything. Where does reason's judgment come in, if faith is whole-hearted adherence?

psalm-o-how-love-i-thy-law.text: O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day

psalm-walk-at-liberty.text: So shall I keep thy law continually for ever and ever. And I will walk at liberty: for I seek thy precepts

psalm-delight-in-the-law.text: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful. But his delight is in the law of the Lord; and in his law doth he meditate day and night. And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper

deuteronomy-for-thy-good.text: And now, Israel, what doth the Lord thy God require of thee, but to fear the Lord thy God, to walk in all his ways, and to love him, and to serve the Lord thy God with all thy heart and with all thy soul, To keep the commandments of the Lord, and his statutes, which I command thee this day for thy good

john-if-ye-love-me.text: If ye love me, keep my commandments

james-perfect-law-of-liberty.text: But whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed

romans-law-is-holy.text: Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good

proverbs-commandment-is-a-lamp.text: For the commandment is a lamp; and the law is light; and reproofs of instruction are the way of life

proverbs-forget-not-my-law.text: My son, forget not my law; but let thine heart keep my commandments: For length of days, and long life, and peace, shall they add to thee

psalm-statutes-my-songs.text: Thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage

matthew-least-commandments.text: Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven

timothy-end-of-the-commandment.text: Now the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned

leviticus-live-in-them.text: Ye shall therefore keep my statutes, and my judgments: which if a man do, he shall live in them: I am the Lord

psalm-thy-word-have-i-hid.text: Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee

quran-desireth-for-you-ease.text: The month of Ramadan in which was revealed the Qur'an, a guidance for mankind, and clear proofs of the guidance, and the Criterion (of right and wrong). And whosoever of you is present, let him fast the month, and whosoever of you is sick or on a journey, (let him fast the same) number of other days. Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you; and (He desireth) that ye should complete the period, and that ye should magnify Allah for having guided you, and that peradventure ye may be thankful.

quran-obey-allah-and-the-messenger.text: O ye who believe! Obey Allah, and obey the messenger and those of you who are in authority; and if ye have a dispute concerning any matter, refer it to Allah and the messenger if ye are (in truth) believers in Allah and the Last Day. That is better and more seemly in the end.

quran-limits-of-allah.text: Divorce must be pronounced twice and then (a woman) must be retained in honour or released in kindness. And it is not lawful for you that ye take from women aught of that which ye have given them; except (in the case) when both fear that they may not be able to keep within the limits (imposed by) Allah. And if ye fear that they may not be able to keep the limits of Allah, in that case it is no sin for either of them if the woman ransom herself. These are the limits (imposed by) Allah. Transgress them not. For whoso transgresseth Allah's limits: such are wrong-doers.

wordsworth-no-prison-is.text: In truth, the prison, unto which we doom / Ourselves, no prison is
wordsworth-no-prison-is.author: William Wordsworth
wordsworth-no-prison-is.work: “Nuns fret not at their convent's narrow room”

locke-where-there-is-no-law.text: the end of law is not to abolish or restrain, but to preserve and enlarge freedom: for in all the states of created beings capable of laws, where there is no law, there is no freedom
locke-where-there-is-no-law.author: John Locke

rousseau-moral-liberty.text: the mere impulse of appetite is slavery, while obedience to a law which we prescribe to ourselves is liberty
rousseau-moral-liberty.author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau

augustine-love-and-do-what-you-will.text: Once for all, then, a short precept is given you: Love, and do what you will
augustine-love-and-do-what-you-will.author: Augustine of Hippo
augustine-love-and-do-what-you-will.work: Homilies on the First Epistle of John

aristotle-law-is-reason.text: Therefore he who bids the law rule may be deemed to bid God and Reason alone rule, but he who bids man rule adds an element of the beast; for desire is a wild beast, and passion perverts the minds of rulers, even when they are the best of men. The law is reason unaffected by desire
aristotle-law-is-reason.author: Aristotle

analects-led-by-laws.text: If the people be led by laws, and uniformity sought to be given them by punishments, they will try to avoid the punishment, but have no sense of shame. "If they be led by virtue, and uniformity sought to be given them by the rules of propriety, they will have the sense of shame, and moreover will become good
analects-led-by-laws.author: Confucius

emerson-no-law-sacred.text: No law can be sacred to me but that of my nature. Good and bad are but names very readily transferable to that or this; the only right is what is after my constitution, the only wrong what is against it
emerson-no-law-sacred.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
